Historically, applying ODI requires meticulous research, structured data modeling, and rigorous analysis. 48: 49: **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** represents a paradigm shift in how AI systems consume and reason over external context. By adopting MCP, we can bridge the gap between static user research and dynamic, agentic AI. 50: 51: The vision for **Agentic ODI** is to build a unified, open protocol where LLMs and autonomous agents can natively query, understand, and reason over ODI data (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and Opportunity Scores) dynamically in real-time. Instead of feeding LLMs disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server will act as the "brain" of customer needs, allowing agents to invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions strictly anchored in verified user outcomes. 52: 53: --- 54: 55: ## 🏗️ Current State (Experimental Testbed) 56: 57: This repository serves as an initial sandbox for understanding server-client MCP communication streams. We are utilizing [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) to prototype HTTP-based context delivery. 58: 59: --- 60: 61: ## 🧩 Code Overview 62: 63: This repository is a [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) made up of **six** installable projects, each with its own `pyproject.toml`, `src/` layout, and tests: 64: 65: | Package | Description | 66: |---|---| 67: | **`core/`** (`agentic-odi-core`) | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, and repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), including ODI opportunity-score computation. | 68: | **`mcp_server/`** (`agentic-odi-mcp-server`) | A foundational MCP Server exposing an HTTP transport layer. It hosts tools for Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, and Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value). | 69: | **`local_server/`** (`agentic-odi-local-server`) | A local FastAPI server that talks to the repository directly (no MCP transport). | 70: | **`client/`** (`agentic-odi-client`) | **The Living Studio** — a spatial, conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation. Provides an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous conversational agent connected to the MCP server. It also hosts `run.py`, the local dev launcher that starts the server and the Studio UI together. | 71: | **`cli/`** (`agentic-odi-cli`) | A [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based command-line interface. It provides version/help plus `outcomes` and `connectors` commands. | 72: | **`connectors/`** (`agentic-odi-connectors`) | Pluggable external integrations. The first kind is an **MCP client connector** that connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP, checks health, and ingests tools/resources into a local ingest sink. Additional kinds (REST, webhooks, and so on) can register against the same protocol later. | 73: 74: --- 75: 76: ## 🚀 Getting Started 77: 78: ### Prerequisites 79: 80: - **Python** 3.10+ 81: - [**uv**](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager 82: 83: Install the entire workspace (all six projects plus dev tooling): 84: 85: ```bash 86: uv sync --all-packages 87: ``` 88: 89: This creates a `.venv` and installs `agentic-odi-core`, `agentic-odi-mcp-server`, `agentic-odi-local-server`, `agentic-odi-client`, `agentic-odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi-connectors` in editable mode. 90: 91: ### 💻 Command-Line Interface (CLI) 92: 93: The [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based CLI lets you interact with Agentic ODI directly from your terminal — no chat UI required. It provides version and help information plus commands for connecting to external systems. Over time it will also expose commands for working with the ODI dataset (Jobs, Steps, and Outcomes). 94: 95: Launch it with: 96: 97: ```bash 98: python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version 99: python -m cli --help # show available options and commands 100: python -m cli # show help when no command is given 101: ``` 102: 103: A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. 104: 105: ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes 106: 107: Manage Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value) via the CLI. The CLI acts as an MCP client, so the server must be running (`python -m mcp_server`): 108: 109: ```bash 110: # Add a Customer Outcome 111: agentic-odi outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" 112: 113: # List outcomes (optionally filtered) 114: agentic-odi outcomes list 115: agentic-odi outcomes list --job-id 116: 117: # Get, update, delete 118: agentic-odi outcomes get 119: agentic-odi outcomes update --importance 9.0 120: agentic-odi outcomes delete --yes 121: 122: # Compute ODI Opportunity Score 123: agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 124: ``` 125: 126: Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` to point to a non-default server if needed. 127: 128: ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) 129: 130: Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. 131: 132: ```bash 133: python -m cli connectors add mcp --name gong --url http://localhost:9000/mcp --tool latest_quote 134: python -m cli connectors list 135: python -m cli connectors health --name gong 136: python -m cli connectors ingest --name gong 137: ``` 138: 139: Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. 140: 141: ### ⚡ One-Command Launch (recommended) 142: 143: `python -m client.run` starts both the MCP server and the Studio UI concurrently. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop both. 144: 145: ```bash 146: python -m client.run 147: ``` 148: 149: | Service | URL | 150: |---|---| 151: | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | 152: | The Living Studio UI | http://localhost:8501 | 153: 154: ### 🔧 Manual Split-Terminal (alternative) 155: 156: Open two terminals and run each process separately: 157: 158: ```bash 159: # Terminal 1 — MCP server 160: python -m mcp_server 161: 162: # Terminal 2 — Streamlit chat UI 163: streamlit run client/src/client/app.py 164: ``` 165: 166: ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) 167: 168: To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: 169: 170: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and 171: - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. 172: 173: A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 174: 175: 1. **Install a local LLM server** 176: 177: Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): 178: 179: ```bash 180: pip install llama-cpp-python 181: ``` 182: 183: 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** 184: 185: Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 186: 187: 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** 188: 189: Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Streamlit client (`client/src/client/app.py`): 190: 191: ```bash 192: python -m llama_cpp.server \ 193: --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ 194: --model_alias local-tools-model \ 195: --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ 196: --chat_format openai 197: ``` 198: 199: This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 200: 201: 4. **Configure the Streamlit client** 202: 203: `client/src/client/app.py` reads the following environment variables (with sensible defaults): 204: 205: | Variable | Default | 206: |---|---| 207: | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | 208: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | 209: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | 210: | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | 211: 212: You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Streamlit sidebar under **"LLM Configuration"**. 213: 214: 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** 215: 216: - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: 217: 218: ```bash 219: curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models 220: ``` 221: 222: If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. 223: 224: - Start the MCP server and Streamlit UI (either via `python -m client.run` or the split-terminal commands above). 225: - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: *"Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository."* 226: - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. 227: - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. 228: 229: ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing 230: 231: Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. 232: 233: --- 234: 235: ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) 236: 237: The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. You can mirror them locally with: 238: 239: ```bash 240: # Ruff lint and formatting checks (per-file config comes from each project's pyproject.toml) 241: uv run ruff check . 242: uv run ruff format --check . 243: 244: # Type checking (run per project so each project's config applies) 245: uv run --directory core mypy . 246: uv run --directory mcp_server mypy . 247: uv run --directory local_server mypy . 248: uv run --directory client mypy . 249: uv run --directory cli mypy . 250: uv run --directory connectors mypy . 251: 252: # Security scanning 253: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src 254: 255: # Tests (same as CI) 256: uv run --directory core pytest 257: uv run --directory mcp_server pytest 258: uv run --directory local_server pytest 259: uv run --directory client pytest 260: uv run --directory cli pytest 261: uv run --directory connectors pytest 262: ``` 263: 264: To run these automatically before each commit, enable the bundled pre-commit hooks: 265: 266: ```bash 267: uv tool install pre-commit 268: pre-commit install 269: ``` 270: 271: After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` will run on staged files whenever you commit. You can also trigger them manually with: 272: 273: ```bash 274: pre-commit run --all-files 275: ``` 276: 277: --- 278: 279: ## ✅ Testing 280: 281: Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely in-memory — no running server required. Each project owns its tests. CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and stores a coverage report as a build artifact: 282: 283: ```bash 284: uv run --directory core pytest 285: uv run --directory mcp_server pytest 286: uv run --directory local_server pytest 287: uv run --directory client pytest 288: uv run --directory cli pytest 289: uv run --directory connectors pytest 290: ``` 291: 292: ### 📊 Test Coverage Map 293: 294: | File | What it covers | 295: |---|---| 296: | `core/tests/test_models.py` | Domain models and ODI opportunity-score computation | 297: | `core/tests/test_service.py` | `ODIService` jobs/steps/outcomes and Customer Outcome CRUD | 298: | `mcp_server/tests/test_odi.py` | Full ODI workflow (add job → steps → outcomes → retrieval) + capabilities tool | 299: | `mcp_server/tests/test_customer_outcomes.py` | Customer Outcomes CRUD, filtering, computed opportunity scores, and tool validation | 300: | `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py` | Error handling and retrieval for the MCP tools | 301: | `mcp_server/tests/test_tools.py` | Tool response-shape contract for `add_job` | 302: | `local_server/tests/test_api.py` | Local FastAPI health endpoint | 303: | `client/tests/test_run.py` | Dev launcher helpers (port checks) | 304: | `cli/tests/test_cli.py` | CLI `--version` and `--help` behavior | 305: | `cli/tests/test_outcomes_cli.py` | Customer Outcomes CLI subcommands with MCP stub | 306: | `cli/tests/test_connectors_cli.py` | CLI `connectors` add/list/health/ingest adapter | 307: | `connectors/tests/test_registry.py` | JSON connector registry persist/load and kind checks | 308: | `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py` | In-memory FastMCP health and ingest records | 309: 310: **Conventions:** 311: 312: - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named `test_*.py`. 313: - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`. 314: - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests. 315: - The server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before each test. 316: 317: > [!TIP] 318: > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the results automatically. 319: 320: ### 🧪 Agent Session Tracking 321: 322: Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview) CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured checkpoints. 323: 324: --- 325: 326: ## 🤝 Superpowers with Pi 327: 328: This project includes [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) as a [Pi package](https://pi.dev/docs/packages). When using [Pi](https://pi.dev) with this project, Superpowers skills and extensions are automatically loaded. 329: 330: To enable: 331: 332: 1. Install Pi: `curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh` 333: 2. Trust the project (first time only): `pi config --local --approve` 334: 3. Start Pi: `pi` 335: 336: The `.pi/settings.json` declares the Superpowers package. The Pi package provides native Pi integration without needing the OpenCode compatibility layer. 343: 344: ### 🧼 Developer Workflow for Formatting 345: 346: - **When editing Python files**, either: 347: - Rely on the **pre-commit hooks** above (recommended), or 348: - Run Ruff formatting directly before pushing: 349: 350: ```bash 351: uv run ruff format . 352: ``` 353: 354: - **CI behavior**: 355: - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files. 356: - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only. 357: - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the changes, and push again. 358: 359: --- 360: 361: ## ☁️ Deployment 362: 363: The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents. 364: 365: ### 🧪 Test Chat (UI) 366: 367: Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser: 368: 369: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)** 370: 371: ### 🔌 MCP Server Endpoint 372: 373: Integrate via the MCP protocol at: 374: 375: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)** 376: 377: > [!IMPORTANT] 378: > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. # Agentic ODI [![CI](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![uv](https://img.shields.io/badge/uv-managed-green)](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) [![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![FastMCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastMCP-powered-orange)](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) [![pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-pytest-blue)](https://pytest.org) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model%20Context%20Protocol-enabled-8A2BE2)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) > **Experimental test to learn and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) specifications.**
--- ## 📋 Table of Contents - [The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation](#-the-vision-context-aware-innovation) - [Current State (Experimental Testbed)](#-current-state-experimental-testbed) - [Code Overview](#-code-overview) - [Getting Started](#-getting-started) - [Command-Line Interface (CLI)](#-command-line-interface-cli) - [Manage Customer Outcomes](#-manage-customer-outcomes) - [External Connectors (MCP Ingest)](#-external-connectors-mcp-ingest) - [One-Command Launch](#-one-command-launch-recommended) - [Manual Split-Terminal](#-manual-split-terminal-alternative) - [Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend](#-local-tools-capable-llm-backend-for-mcp-testing) - [Agent-Driven Testing](#-agent-driven-testing) - [Linting, Formatting & Type Checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) - [Testing](#-testing) - [Test Coverage Map](#-test-coverage-map) - [Agent Session Tracking](#-agent-session-tracking) - [Superpowers with Pi](#-superpowers-with-pi) - [Developer Workflow for Formatting](#-developer-workflow-for-formatting) - [Deployment](#-deployment) - [Roadmap & Next Steps](#-roadmap--next-steps) - [Contributing](#-contributing) - [License](#-license) --- ## 🌟 The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation **Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)**, built on the "Jobs-to-be-Done" theory, relies on deeply understanding customer needs, desired outcomes, and execution contexts. Historically, applying ODI requires meticulous research, structured data modeling, and rigorous analysis. **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** represents a paradigm shift in how AI systems consume and reason over external context. By adopting MCP, we can bridge the gap between static user research and dynamic, agentic AI. The vision for **Agentic ODI** is to build a unified, open protocol where LLMs and autonomous agents can natively query, understand, and reason over ODI data (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and Opportunity Scores) dynamically in real-time. Instead of feeding LLMs disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server will act as the "brain" of customer needs, allowing agents to invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions strictly anchored in verified user outcomes. --- ## 🏗️ Current State (Experimental Testbed) This repository serves as an initial sandbox for understanding server-client MCP communication streams. We are utilizing [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) to prototype HTTP-based context delivery. --- ## 🧩 Code Overview This repository is a [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) made up of **six** installable projects, each with its own `pyproject.toml`, `src/` layout, and tests: | Package | Description | |---|---| | **`core/`** (`agentic-odi-core`) | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, and repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), including ODI opportunity-score computation. | | **`mcp_server/`** (`agentic-odi-mcp-server`) | A foundational MCP Server exposing an HTTP transport layer. It hosts tools for Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, and Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value). | | **`local_server/`** (`agentic-odi-local-server`) | A local FastAPI server that talks to the repository directly (no MCP transport). | | **`client/`** (`agentic-odi-client`) | **The Living Studio** — a spatial, conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation. Provides an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous conversational agent connected to the MCP server. It also hosts `run.py`, the local dev launcher that starts the server and the Studio UI together. | | **`cli/`** (`agentic-odi-cli`) | A [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based command-line interface. It provides version/help plus `outcomes` and `connectors` commands. | | **`connectors/`** (`agentic-odi-connectors`) | Pluggable external integrations. The first kind is an **MCP client connector** that connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP, checks health, and ingests tools/resources into a local ingest sink. Additional kinds (REST, webhooks, and so on) can register against the same protocol later. | --- ## 🚀 Getting Started ### Prerequisites - **Python** 3.10+ - [**uv**](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager Install the entire workspace (all six projects plus dev tooling): ```bash uv sync --all-packages ``` This creates a `.venv` and installs `agentic-odi-core`, `agentic-odi-mcp-server`, `agentic-odi-local-server`, `agentic-odi-client`, `agentic-odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi-connectors` in editable mode. ### 💻 Command-Line Interface (CLI) The [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based CLI lets you interact with Agentic ODI directly from your terminal — no chat UI required. It provides version and help information plus commands for connecting to external systems. Over time it will also expose commands for working with the ODI dataset (Jobs, Steps, and Outcomes). Launch it with: ```bash python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m cli --help # show available options and commands python -m cli # show help when no command is given ``` A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes Manage Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value) via the CLI. The CLI acts as an MCP client, so the server must be running (`python -m mcp_server`): ```bash # Add a Customer Outcome agentic-odi outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" # List outcomes (optionally filtered) agentic-odi outcomes list agentic-odi outcomes list --job-id # Get, update, delete agentic-odi outcomes get agentic-odi outcomes update --importance 9.0 agentic-odi outcomes delete --yes # Compute ODI Opportunity Score agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 ``` Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` to point to a non-default server if needed. ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. ```bash python -m cli connectors add mcp --name gong --url http://localhost:9000/mcp --tool latest_quote python -m cli connectors list python -m cli connectors health --name gong python -m cli connectors ingest --name gong ``` Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. ### ⚡ One-Command Launch (recommended) `python -m client.run` starts both the MCP server and the Studio UI concurrently. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop both. ```bash python -m client.run ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | The Living Studio UI | http://localhost:8501 | ### 🔧 Manual Split-Terminal (alternative) Open two terminals and run each process separately: ```bash # Terminal 1 — MCP server python -m mcp_server # Terminal 2 — Streamlit chat UI streamlit run client/src/client/app.py ``` ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 1. **Install a local LLM server** Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): ```bash pip install llama-cpp-python ``` 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Streamlit client (`client/src/client/app.py`): ```bash python -m llama_cpp.server \ --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ --model_alias local-tools-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ --chat_format openai ``` This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 4. **Configure the Streamlit client** `client/src/client/app.py` reads the following environment variables (with sensible defaults): | Variable | Default | |---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Streamlit sidebar under **"LLM Configuration"**. 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models ``` If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. - Start the MCP server and Streamlit UI (either via `python -m client.run` or the split-terminal commands above). - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: *"Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository."* - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. --- ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. You can mirror them locally with: ```bash # Ruff lint and formatting checks (per-file config comes from each project's pyproject.toml) uv run ruff check . uv run ruff format --check . # Type checking (run per project so each project's config applies) uv run --directory core mypy . uv run --directory mcp_server mypy . uv run --directory local_server mypy . uv run --directory client mypy . uv run --directory cli mypy . uv run --directory connectors mypy . # Security scanning uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src # Tests (same as CI) uv run --directory core pytest uv run --directory mcp_server pytest uv run --directory local_server pytest uv run --directory client pytest uv run --directory cli pytest uv run --directory connectors pytest ``` To run these automatically before each commit, enable the bundled pre-commit hooks: ```bash uv tool install pre-commit pre-commit install ``` After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` will run on staged files whenever you commit. You can also trigger them manually with: ```bash pre-commit run --all-files ``` --- ## ✅ Testing Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely in-memory — no running server required. Each project owns its tests. CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and stores a coverage report as a build artifact: ```bash uv run --directory core pytest uv run --directory mcp_server pytest uv run --directory local_server pytest uv run --directory client pytest uv run --directory cli pytest uv run --directory connectors pytest ``` ### 📊 Test Coverage Map | File | What it covers | |---|---| | `core/tests/test_models.py` | Domain models and ODI opportunity-score computation | | `core/tests/test_service.py` | `ODIService` jobs/steps/outcomes and Customer Outcome CRUD | | `mcp_server/tests/test_odi.py` | Full ODI workflow (add job → steps → outcomes → retrieval) + capabilities tool | | `mcp_server/tests/test_customer_outcomes.py` | Customer Outcomes CRUD, filtering, computed opportunity scores, and tool validation | | `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py` | Error handling and retrieval for the MCP tools | | `mcp_server/tests/test_tools.py` | Tool response-shape contract for `add_job` | | `local_server/tests/test_api.py` | Local FastAPI health endpoint | | `client/tests/test_run.py` | Dev launcher helpers (port checks) | | `cli/tests/test_cli.py` | CLI `--version` and `--help` behavior | | `cli/tests/test_outcomes_cli.py` | Customer Outcomes CLI subcommands with MCP stub | | `cli/tests/test_connectors_cli.py` | CLI `connectors` add/list/health/ingest adapter | | `connectors/tests/test_registry.py` | JSON connector registry persist/load and kind checks | | `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py` | In-memory FastMCP health and ingest records | **Conventions:** - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named `test_*.py`. - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`. - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests. - The server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before each test. > [!TIP] > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the results automatically. ### 🧪 Agent Session Tracking Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview) CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured checkpoints. --- ## 🤝 Superpowers with Pi This project includes [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) as a [Pi package](https://pi.dev/docs/packages). When using [Pi](https://pi.dev) with this project, Superpowers skills and extensions are automatically loaded. To enable: 1. Install Pi: `curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh` 2. Trust the project (first time only): `pi config --local --approve` 3. Start Pi: `pi` The `.pi/settings.json` declares the Superpowers package. Pi will clone it and load: - **Extension**: `superpowers.ts` — injects the `using-superpowers` bootstrap at session startup and after compaction - **Skills**: 12 Superpowers skills (TDD, subagent-driven-development, systematic-debugging, etc.) > [!NOTE] > Superpowers is also available for OpenCode via the plugin in `opencode.json`. The Pi package provides native Pi integration without needing the OpenCode compatibility layer. ### 🧼 Developer Workflow for Formatting - **When editing Python files**, either: - Rely on the **pre-commit hooks** above (recommended), or - Run Ruff formatting directly before pushing: ```bash uv run ruff format . ``` - **CI behavior**: - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files. - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only. - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the changes, and push again. --- ## ☁️ Deployment The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents. ### 🧪 Test Chat (UI) Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)** ### 🔌 MCP Server Endpoint Integrate via the MCP protocol at: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)** > [!IMPORTANT] > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a client. --- ## 🗺️ Roadmap & Next Steps As we validate the feasibility of this architecture, our next milestones include: - [x] **External MCP client connector**: Pluggable connectors package with an HTTP MCP ingest client, CLI adapter, and in-memory tests. - [ ] **Map ingested evidence onto ODI artifacts**: Turn connector records into jobs, outcomes, or evidence without mixing connector plumbing into the ODI store. - [ ] **Additional connector kinds**: REST/webhooks and similar integrations implementing the same `Connector` protocol. - [ ] **ODI Schema Definition**: Define standardized Pydantic models for *Jobs*, *Steps*, and *Outcomes*. - [x] **CLI Dataset Commands**: Extend `cli/` so the ODI dataset can be created, queried, and scored from the terminal, in addition to the current MCP path. - [ ] **Context Tooling**: Replace the dummy `greet` tool with capabilities like `get_job_map(job_id)` or `evaluate_outcome(statement)`. - [ ] **Data Persistence Layer**: Connect the fastmcp server to a lightweight vector or relational database containing actual user research data. - [ ] **Agentic Integration**: Hook the client up to an LLM (e.g., via LangChain or standard OpenAI clients) so the LLM can *discover* the ODI tools and intelligently request customer insights when ideating features. --- ## 🤝 Contributing Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Please ensure any change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) before opening a pull request. --- ## 📄 License No license has been specified for this repository yet. Until one is added, all rights reserved by the maintainers. Please reach out before reuse or redistribution. ---
*Let's build AI that builds what people actually need.*

    pieces=[]

    for line in re.finditer(rb'\[(.*?)\]\s*TJ|\((?:[^()\\]|\\.)*\)\s*Tj', dec, re.DOTALL):
        pass
    # simpler: extract all literal strings
    txt=''
    for t in re.finditer(rb'\((?:[^()\\]|\\.)*\)', dec):
        s=t.group(0)[1:-1]
        s=s.replace(b'\\(',b'(').replace(b'\\)',b')').replace(b'\\\\',b'\\')
        txt+=s.decode('latin-1')
    # hex strings
    for t in re.finditer(rb'<([0-9A-Fa-f\s]+)>', dec):

        try:
            b=bytes.fromhex(h.decode())
            txt+=' '+b.decode('utf-16-be','ignore')
        except Exception: pass
    if txt.strip():

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

from connectors.models import HealthStatus, IngestBatch, IngestRecord
from typer.testing import CliRunner

from cli.cli import app

ANSI_ESCAPE = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m")
runner = CliRunner()


def _strip(text: str) -> str:
    return ANSI_ESCAPE.sub("", text)


def test_connectors_help_lists_commands() -> None:
    result = runner.invoke(app, ["connectors", "--help"])

    assert result.exit_code == 0
    output = _strip(result.output)
    assert "list" in output
    assert "add" in output
    assert "health" in output
    assert "ingest" in output


def test_connectors_list_empty(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    result = runner.invoke(app, ["connectors", "list", "--config", str(config)])

    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert "No connectors configured." in _strip(result.output)


def test_connectors_add_mcp_then_list(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    add = runner.invoke(
        app,
        [
            "connectors",
            "add",
            "mcp",
            "--name",
            "gong",
            "--url",
            "http://localhost:9000/mcp",
            "--config",
            str(config),
        ],
    )
    listed = runner.invoke(app, ["connectors", "list", "--config", str(config)])

    assert add.exit_code == 0
    assert listed.exit_code == 0
    assert "gong" in _strip(listed.output)
    assert "mcp" in _strip(listed.output)
    payload = json.loads(config.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    assert payload["connectors"][0]["settings"]["url"] == "http://localhost:9000/mcp"


def test_connectors_add_rejects_duplicate(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    args = [
        "connectors",
        "add",
        "mcp",
        "--name",
        "gong",
        "--url",
        "http://localhost:9000/mcp",
        "--config",
        str(config),
    ]
    runner.invoke(app, args)
    result = runner.invoke(app, args)

    assert result.exit_code == 1
    assert "already exists" in _strip(result.output)


def test_connectors_add_rejects_unknown_kind(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    result = runner.invoke(
        app,
        ["connectors", "add", "rest", "--name", "jira", "--config", str(config)],
    )

    assert result.exit_code == 1
    assert "Unknown connector kind" in _strip(result.output)


def test_connectors_add_mcp_requires_url(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    result = runner.invoke(
        app,
        ["connectors", "add", "mcp", "--name", "gong", "--config", str(config)],
    )

    assert result.exit_code == 1
    assert "--url is required" in _strip(result.output)


class _FakeConnector:
    def __init__(self, batch: IngestBatch | None = None) -> None:
        self.batch = batch or IngestBatch(connector_name="gong")

    async def health(self) -> HealthStatus:
        return HealthStatus(ok=True, message="reachable")

    async def ingest(self) -> IngestBatch:
        return self.batch


def test_connectors_health_uses_built_connector(tmp_path: Path, monkeypatch) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    runner.invoke(
        app,
        [
            "connectors",
            "add",
            "mcp",
            "--name",
            "gong",
            "--url",
            "http://localhost:9000/mcp",
            "--config",
            str(config),
        ],
    )
    monkeypatch.setattr("cli.connectors.build_connector", lambda _config: _FakeConnector())

    result = runner.invoke(app, ["connectors", "health", "--name", "gong", "--config", str(config)])

    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert "reachable" in _strip(result.output)


def test_connectors_ingest_appends_to_sink(tmp_path: Path, monkeypatch) -> None:
    config = tmp_path / "connectors.json"
    runner.invoke(
        app,
        [
            "connectors",
            "add",
            "mcp",
            "--name",
            "gong",
            "--url",
            "http://localhost:9000/mcp",
            "--config",
            str(config),
        ],
    )
    batch = IngestBatch(
        connector_name="gong",
        records=[
            IngestRecord(
                source_name="gong",
                source_kind="mcp",
                item_type="catalog",
                name="mcp-catalog",
                content="{}",
            )
        ],
    )
    sink = MagicMock()
    monkeypatch.setattr("cli.connectors.build_connector", lambda _config: _FakeConnector(batch))
    monkeypatch.setattr("cli.connectors.get_default_sink", lambda: sink)

    result = runner.invoke(app, ["connectors", "ingest", "--name", "gong", "--config", str(config)])

    assert result.exit_code == 0
    sink.append.assert_called_once()
    assert "gong" in _strip(result.output)

1: # Bundled CLI Distribution & Self-Update — Design
2: 
3: Date: 2026-10-15
4: Status: Approved (design); implementation plan pending
5: 
6: ## Intent and why
7: 
8: Today the `agentic-odi` CLI is consumed by installing the whole `uv`
9: workspace in editable mode. We want a world-class, "state-of-the-art"
10: binary distribution: a self-contained executable that a user installs with
11: a single `curl … | sh` and that keeps itself current without the user
12: managing a Python toolchain.
13: 
14: This mirrors the experience of `gh`, `deno`, `bun`, and `ollama`: install
15: with a one-liner, get a native-feeling command, and receive updates without
16: thinking about it.
17: 
18: ## Goals
19: 
20: - A self-contained artifact per platform with **near-instant startup**.
21: - One-line install: `curl -fsSL <url>/install.sh | sh` (and a PowerShell
22:   equivalent for Windows).
23: - **Automatic background updates, on by default**, plus an explicit
24:   user-invoked update command.
25: - Automated versioning and release/tag creation driven by CI.
26: - Support Linux (x86_64, arm64), macOS (x86_64, arm64), Windows (x86_64).
27: 
28: ## Non-goals
29: 
30: - Code signing / notarization (deferred; document the workarounds).
31: - Packaging the MCP server / local server / chat client as binaries (this is
32:   about the CLI only).
33: - Publishing to PyPI as the primary distribution channel.
34: - A vanity download domain (use GitHub Releases for now).
35: 
36: ## Anti-goals (what would make this a failure even if it "works")
37: 
38: - Shipping a build that crashes on `--backend mcp` because a dependency was
39:   stripped for size.
40: - An auto-updater that blocks or slows a command when offline.
41: - An updater that can corrupt an install if interrupted (non-atomic swap).
42: - Replacing a running executable in place (fails on Windows; races on unix).
43: 
44: ## Constraints
45: 
46: - The CLI is a Python package (`agentic-odi-cli`) in a `uv` workspace with
47:   six members. Once bundled, the CLI no longer depends on the workspace at
48:   runtime; the source tree keeps its current editable-install workflow.
49: - The CLI defaults to a local SQLite backend (`AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND=local`),
50:   so the binary is useful standalone. MCP is opt-in (`--backend mcp`).
51: - The CLI imports `fastmcp` at module top (`cli/src/cli/outcomes.py`), which
52:   pulls a large tree (mcp, httpx, starlette, uvicorn). `pydantic` v2 pulls
53:   compiled `pydantic-core`. These are the bundling risk points.
54: - No git tags exist today; `cli/src/cli/version.py` hardcodes `0.1.0`.
55: - Reproduction of the current runner matrix: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, macOS,
56:   and Windows runners.
57: 
58: ## Decisions (made by the human partner unless noted)
59: 
60: 1. **Bundler: PyInstaller `--onedir`, shipped as a compressed archive.**
61:    `--onefile` re-extracts to a temp dir on every invocation and adds
62:    ~0.5–1.5s startup latency; `--onedir` starts near-instantly. We accept
63:    "one downloadable archive, installed into a versioned directory" instead
64:    of "one literal file." Nuitka is the fallback if PyInstaller proves
65:    unusable.
66: 2. **No code signing for now.** Document Gatekeeper (macOS) and SmartScreen
67:    (Windows) workarounds in the README.
68: 3. **Background auto-update is ON by default**, applied on the next run,
69:    with opt-out (flag/env). Also expose explicit `odi update`.
70: 4. **Binary size: full functionality, optimized.** *It just works* beats
71:    *small* (builder's call). Bundle everything so `--backend mcp` works out
72:    of the box. Optimize with strip/exclusions. **No UPX** (AV false
73:    positives). Because onedir has no per-run extraction cost, size is only a
74:    download-time concern. Revisit a lazy `fastmcp` import only if measured
75:    size is egregious *and* the MCP backend keeps working.
76: 5. **Versioning: semver primary + release datetime secondary.**
77:    Git tag is `v<semver>`; the build also embeds the release datetime (UTC)
78:    so users can see *when* a version was released.
79: 6. **Command names:** primary `odi`; additionally `odipm` and `odi-cli`;
80:    keep `agentic-odi` for backward compatibility.
81: 
82: ## The how (decided)
83: 
84: ### Artifact
85: 
86: - PyInstaller **onedir** build producing an executable named `odi`
87:   (`odi.exe` on Windows) plus its `_internal/` support directory.
88: - Packaged per platform:
89:   - unix: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz`
90:   - windows: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`
91: - `os`/`arch` tokens: `linux/x86_64`, `linux/arm64`, `macos/x86_64`,
92:   `macos/arm64`, `windows/x86_64`.
93: - A `checksums.txt` (SHA-256) is published alongside the archives.
94: 
95: ### Install layout
96: 
97: ```
98: ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
99:   versions/0.1.0/            # extracted onedir bundle (odi + _internal/)
100:   versions/0.2.0/
101:   current -> versions/0.2.0  # atomic symlink; flipping it IS the update
102: ~/.local/bin/
103:   odi         -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
104:   odipm       -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
105:   odi-cli     -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
106:   agentic-odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
107: ~/.config/agentic-odi/update.json   # last-check time + state
108: ```
109: 
110: - Install root overridable via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
111: - Both `share` and `bin` roots derive from XDG (`XDG_DATA_HOME`,
112:   `XDG_BIN_HOME`) with sensible fallbacks. Use `platformdirs` or hand-rolled
113:   XDG resolution (builder's call).
114: - **Windows:** no symlinks. Install to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agentic-odi\`; ship
115:   `odi.exe` plus `odipm.exe`, `odi-cli.exe`, `agentic-odi.exe` copies.
116:   Updates use a deferred helper process so the running `.exe` can be
117:   swapped.
118: 
119: ### Update mechanism
120: 
121: - `cli/update.py` module providing:
122:   - `check_for_update()` → query GitHub Releases "latest"; semver-compare
123:     against the embedded version.
124:   - `resolve_asset()` → map runtime OS/arch to the correct asset name.
125:   - `verify_checksum()` → SHA-256 verify against `checksums.txt`.
126:   - `perform_update()` → download → verify → extract to
127:     `versions/<new>` → **atomically** re-point `current`.
128:   - A **lockfile** guards concurrent updates.
129: - **Auto path:** on launch, at most one network check per 24h (cached in
130:   `update.json`). If newer, download + verify + extract + flip in a
131:   background thread, then print
132:   `Updated to vX.Y.Z — takes effect next run`. Never blocks the command;
133:   network failures are swallowed.
134: - **Suppressed when:** not a frozen build (running from source), env
135:   `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1`, global flag `--no-update`, non-interactive
136:   context, lock held, or install location not writable.
137: - **Explicit path:** `odi update [--check] [--force] [--version X.Y.Z]
138:   [--now]`. `--now` re-execs into the newly installed version.
139: - Updates are never applied to a running process; they apply on next launch.
140: 
141: ### Versioning & naming
142: 
143: - Single source of truth = the git tag `vX.Y.Z`.
144: - Build step injects a generated `_build_info.py` with:
145:   `VERSION = "0.1.0"`, `RELEASE_DATE_UTC = "2026-10-15T21:13:00Z"`,
146:   `COMMIT = "<sha>"`, `TARGET = "<os>-<arch>"`.
147: - `cli/version.py` reads from `_build_info` (falling back for editable/dev
148:   installs).
149: - `odi --version` → `0.1.0 (2026-10-15)`.
150: - `odi --version --verbose` → adds commit SHA, build date, target triple.
151: 
152: ### CI / tagging
153: 
154: - **release-please** (Conventional Commits) maintains a release PR that
155:   bumps the version and updates the changelog. Merging it creates the tag
156:   `vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub Release.
157: - A single **root component** version for the whole repo (one product
158:   version), not per-package versions.
159: - `release.yml` triggers on tag push → matrix build → uploads archives +
160:   `checksums.txt` + `install.sh` + `install.ps1` to the Release → publishes.
161: 
162: | Runner | Target |
163: |---|---|
164: | `ubuntu-latest` | linux-x86_64 |
165: | `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | linux-arm64 |
166: | `macos-14` | macos-arm64 |
167: | `macos-13` (or Rosetta on 14) | macos-x86_64 |
168: | `windows-latest` | windows-x86_64 |
169: 
170: ## Phasing
171: 
172: 1. **Spike (highest risk):** PyInstaller `--onedir` bundle the CLI on Linux;
173:    run `--version`, `--help`, `outcomes add` against both backends. Confirms
174:    `pydantic-core` + `fastmcp` bundle cleanly and startup is fast.
175: 2. `_build_info` injection + `cli/update.py` + `odi update` command +
176:    startup hook, with unit tests (semver compare, OS/arch→asset resolution,
177:    checksum verify, cache/lock, atomic flip).
178: 3. `install.sh` / `install.ps1` (aliases, PATH, completions).
179: 4. release-please config + `release.yml` matrix + checksums.
180: 5. README install/update docs + end-to-end test installing from a real
181:    tagged Release.
182: 
183: ## Flagged wrinkles
184: 
185: - **macOS Intel builds:** `macos-13` is the last x86_64 runner and is being
186:   retired; fallback is an x86_64 build under Rosetta on `macos-14`. May
187:   force a "drop Intel Mac" decision later.
188: - **Auto-update assumes a writable home.** Under system-wide installs
189:   (`/usr/local/bin`, package managers) auto-update is disabled; only the
190:   install script manages those.
191: - **Offline behavior:** auto-update must always no-op gracefully and never
192:   block or slow a command.
193: - **`fastmcp` weight:** bundled for correctness; size revisited only if
194:   measured and if the MCP backend can stay functional.
195: 
196: ## Left to the builder
197: 
198: - Exact PyInstaller spec / hidden-import hooks and exclusion list.
199: - Exact `platformdirs` vs hand-rolled XDG resolution.
200: - Exact lockfile mechanism (file lock vs atomic O_EXCL).
201: - Windows deferred-swap implementation details.
202: - release-please configuration specifics.
203:

205: 
206: 1. Keep `agentic-odi` as an alias alongside `odi` / `odipm` / `odi-cli`.
207: 2. Release assets live on GitHub Releases (`alehar9320/agentic-odi`) for now.

|---|---|
| `ubuntu-latest` | linux-x86_64 |
| `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | linux-arm64 |

# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

"""Append-only Intent Store (CTO specification)."""

import json
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime


class IntentStore:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "intent_store.db") -> None:
        # Connect to SQLite in WAL mode for high-performance concurrency
        self.conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
        self.conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self) -> None:
        """Creates an immutable, append-only event table."""
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute(
                """
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL,
                    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    payload TEXT NOT NULL
                )
            """
            )

    def append(self, event_type: str, payload: dict) -> None:
        """Appends a new event to the stream (Immutable write)."""
        timestamp = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        payload_json = json.dumps(payload)
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute(
                "INSERT INTO events (timestamp, event_type, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                (timestamp, event_type, payload_json),
            )

    def get_stream(self) -> list[dict]:
        """Retrieves the full chronological event stream for AI reasoning."""
        cursor = self.conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute("SELECT id, timestamp, event_type, payload FROM events ORDER BY id ASC")
        return [
            {
                "id": row[0],
                "timestamp": row[1],
                "type": row[2],
                "payload": json.loads(row[3]) if row[3] else {},
            }
            for row in cursor.fetchall()
        ]

    def clear(self) -> None:
        """Clear all events (for testing)."""
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute("DELETE FROM events")

    def close(self) -> None:
        self.conn.close()

@@ -1,239 +1,248 @@
 # Bundled CLI Distribution & Self-Update — Design
 
 Date: 2026-10-15
 Status: Approved (design); implementation plan pending
 
 ## Intent and why
 
 Today the `agentic-odi` CLI is consumed by installing the whole `uv`
 workspace in editable mode. We want a world-class, "state-of-the-art"
 binary distribution: a self-contained executable that a user installs with
 a single `curl … | sh` and that keeps itself current without the user
 managing a Python toolchain.
 
 This mirrors the experience of `gh`, `deno`, `bun`, and `ollama`: install
 with a one-liner, get a native-feeling command, and receive updates without
 thinking about it.
 
 ## Goals
 
 - A self-contained artifact per platform with **near-instant startup**.
 - One-line install: `curl -fsSL <url>/install.sh | sh` (and a PowerShell
   equivalent for Windows).
 - **Automatic background updates, on by default**, plus an explicit
   user-invoked update command.
 - Automated versioning and release/tag creation driven by CI.
 - Support Linux (x86_64, arm64), macOS (x86_64, arm64), Windows (x86_64).
 
 ## Non-goals
 
 - Code signing / notarization (deferred; document the workarounds).
 - Packaging the MCP server / local server / chat client as binaries (this is
   about the CLI only).
 - Publishing to PyPI as the primary distribution channel.
 - A vanity download domain (use GitHub Releases for now).
 
 ## Anti-goals (what would make this a failure even if it "works")
 
 - Shipping a build that crashes on `--backend mcp` because a dependency was
   stripped for size.
 - An auto-updater that blocks or slows a command when offline.
 - An updater that can corrupt an install if interrupted (non-atomic swap).
 - Replacing a running executable in place (fails on Windows; races on unix).
 
 ## Constraints
 
 - The CLI is a Python package (`agentic-odi-cli`) in a `uv` workspace with
   six members. Once bundled, the CLI no longer depends on the workspace at
   runtime; the source tree keeps its current editable-install workflow.
 - **Correction found during design review:** although a `LocalBackend` exists
   (`cli/src/cli/backend.py`), every `outcomes` command currently hardcodes the
   MCP backend (`get_backend("mcp", …)`, and `score` calls `_call_mcp`
   directly). `LocalBackend` is unreachable and there is no `--backend` flag.
   So the CLI as shipped effectively requires a running MCP server. Wiring the
   local backend up and exposing `--backend {local,mcp}` is **in scope** (see
   Decision 7) so the binary is genuinely useful standalone.
 - The CLI imports `fastmcp` at module top (`cli/src/cli/outcomes.py`), which
   pulls a large tree (mcp, httpx, starlette, uvicorn). `pydantic` v2 pulls
   compiled `pydantic-core`. These are the bundling risk points.
 - No git tags exist today; `cli/src/cli/version.py` hardcodes `0.1.0`.
 - Reproduction of the current runner matrix: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, macOS,
   and Windows runners.
 
 ## Decisions (made by the human partner unless noted)
 
 1. **Bundler: PyInstaller `--onedir`, shipped as a compressed archive.**
    `--onefile` re-extracts to a temp dir on every invocation and adds
    ~0.5–1.5s startup latency; `--onedir` starts near-instantly. We accept
    "one downloadable archive, installed into a versioned directory" instead
    of "one literal file." Nuitka is the fallback if PyInstaller proves
    unusable.
 2. **No code signing for now.** Document Gatekeeper (macOS) and SmartScreen
    (Windows) workarounds in the README.
 3. **Background auto-update is ON by default**, applied on the next run,
    with opt-out (flag/env). Also expose explicit `odi update`.
 4. **Binary size: full functionality, optimized.** *It just works* beats
    *small* (builder's call). Bundle everything so `--backend mcp` works out
    of the box. Optimize with strip/exclusions. **No UPX** (AV false
    positives). Because onedir has no per-run extraction cost, size is only a
    download-time concern. **Concrete threshold (builder's call):** if the
    compressed per-platform archive exceeds **~80 MB**, add the lazy-`fastmcp`
    work in Phase 2 *only if* the MCP backend still works in the frozen binary;
    otherwise keep it bundled and accept the size.
 5. **Versioning: semver primary + release datetime secondary.**
    Git tag is `v<semver>`; the build also embeds the release datetime (UTC)
    so users can see *when* a version was released.
 6. **Command names:** primary `odi`; additionally `odipm` and `odi-cli`;
    keep `agentic-odi` for backward compatibility.
 7. **Wire up the local backend + a `--backend {local,mcp}` flag** so the
    binary works standalone out of the box (human partner's call; see the
    correction under Constraints). This is a functional change to
    `cli/src/cli/outcomes.py` and `cli/src/cli/backend.py`, included in the
    plan. `local` is the default; `mcp` preserves today's behavior.
 8. **Linux compatibility floor: glibc 2.17-class.** Linux artifacts are built
    inside an old-glibc container (manylinux2014 / Ubuntu 20.04) so they run on
    virtually all current distros, not just the runner's glibc (human
    partner's call). Adds a container step to the Linux build jobs.
 
 ## The how (decided)
 
 ### Artifact
 
 - PyInstaller **onedir** build producing an executable named `odi`
   (`odi.exe` on Windows) plus its `_internal/` support directory.
 - Packaged per platform:
   - unix: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz`
   - windows: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`
 - `os`/`arch` tokens: `linux/x86_64`, `linux/arm64`, `macos/x86_64`,
   `macos/arm64`, `windows/x86_64`.
 - A `checksums.txt` (SHA-256) is published alongside the archives.
 
 ### Install layout
 
 ```
 ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
   versions/0.1.0/            # extracted onedir bundle (odi + _internal/)
   versions/0.2.0/
   current -> versions/0.2.0  # atomic symlink; flipping it IS the update
 ~/.local/bin/
   odi         -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
   odipm       -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
   odi-cli     -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
   agentic-odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
 ~/.config/agentic-odi/update.json   # last-check time + state
 ```
 
 - Install root overridable via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
 - Both `share` and `bin` roots derive from XDG (`XDG_DATA_HOME`,
   `XDG_BIN_HOME`) with sensible fallbacks. Use `platformdirs` or hand-rolled
   XDG resolution (builder's call).
 - **v1 is user-local only — no sudo / system-wide mode.** The installer never
   escalates and never writes to `/usr/local`. System-wide installs are out of
   scope for v1 (builder's call); if added later, they become install-script
   managed with auto-update disabled.
 - **Windows:** no symlinks. Install to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agentic-odi\`; ship
   `odi.exe` plus `odipm.exe`, `odi-cli.exe`, `agentic-odi.exe` copies.
   Updates use a deferred helper process so the running `.exe` can be swapped.
   **Fallback (builder's call):** if the Phase 1 spike shows the deferred swap
   cannot be made safe, Windows auto-apply falls back to check-only with an
   "update available" notice, and `odi update` becomes the apply path on
   Windows. The anti-goal (never corrupt an install) wins over auto-on-by-default.
 
 ### Update mechanism
 
 - `cli/update.py` module providing:
   - `check_for_update()` → query GitHub Releases "latest"; semver-compare
     against the embedded version.
   - `resolve_asset()` → map runtime OS/arch to the correct asset name.
   - `verify_checksum()` → SHA-256 verify against `checksums.txt`.
   - `perform_update()` → download → verify → extract to
     `versions/<new>` → **atomically** re-point `current`.
   - A **lockfile** guards concurrent updates.
 - **Auto path:** on launch, at most one network check per 24h (cached in
   `update.json`). If newer, download + verify + extract + flip in a
   background thread, then print
   `Updated to vX.Y.Z — takes effect next run`. Never blocks the command;
   network failures are swallowed.
 - **Suppressed when:** not a frozen build (running from source), env
   `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1`, global flag `--no-update`, non-interactive
   context, lock held, or install location not writable.
 - **Explicit path:** `odi update [--check] [--force] [--version X.Y.Z]
   [--now]`. `--now` re-execs into the newly installed version.
 - Updates are never applied to a running process; they apply on next launch.
 
 ### Versioning & naming
 
 - Single source of truth = the git tag `vX.Y.Z`.
 - Build step injects a generated `_build_info.py` with:
   `VERSION = "0.1.0"`, `RELEASE_DATE_UTC = "2026-10-15T21:13:00Z"`,
   `COMMIT = "<sha>"`, `TARGET = "<os>-<arch>"`.
 - `cli/version.py` reads from `_build_info` (falling back for editable/dev
   installs).
 - `odi --version` → `0.1.0 (2026-10-15)`.
 - `odi --version --verbose` → adds commit SHA, build date, target triple.
 
 ### CI / tagging
 
 - **release-please** (Conventional Commits) maintains a release PR that
   bumps the version and updates the changelog. Merging it creates the tag
   `vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub Release.
 - A single **root component** version for the whole repo (one product
   version), not per-package versions.
 - **First release is `0.1.0`** (builder's call): with no prior tags and a
   commit history that would otherwise make release-please derive a higher
   number, pin the baseline explicitly (release-please `initial-version` /
   bootstrap tag) so the first `curl | sh` user gets `0.1.0` matching
   `version.py`.
 - `release.yml` triggers on tag push → matrix build → uploads archives +
   `checksums.txt` + `install.sh` + `install.ps1` to the Release → publishes.
 
 | Runner | Target | Notes |
 |---|---|---|
 | `ubuntu-latest` | linux-x86_64 | build inside old-glibc container |
 | `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | linux-arm64 | build inside old-glibc container |
 | `macos-14` | macos-arm64 | |
 | `macos-13` (or Rosetta on 14) | macos-x86_64 | see flagged wrinkles |
 | `windows-latest` | windows-x86_64 | |
 
 Linux jobs run PyInstaller inside a manylinux2014 / Ubuntu 20.04 container
 (glibc 2.17-class) to maximize distro compatibility (Decision 8).
 
 ## Phasing
 
 1. **Spike (highest risk):** PyInstaller `--onedir` bundle the CLI on Linux;
    run `--version`, `--help`, `outcomes add` against both backends. Confirms
    `pydantic-core` + `fastmcp` bundle cleanly and startup is fast.
 2. `_build_info` injection + `cli/update.py` + `odi update` command +
    startup hook, with unit tests (semver compare, OS/arch→asset resolution,
    checksum verify, cache/lock, atomic flip).
 3. `install.sh` / `install.ps1` (aliases, PATH, completions).
 4. release-please config + `release.yml` matrix + checksums.
 5. README install/update docs + end-to-end test installing from a real
    tagged Release.
 
 ## Flagged wrinkles
 
 - **macOS Intel builds:** `macos-13` is the last x86_64 runner and is being
   retired; fallback is an x86_64 build under Rosetta on `macos-14`. May
   force a "drop Intel Mac" decision later.
-- **Auto-update assumes a writable home.** Under system-wide installs
-  (`/usr/local/bin`, package managers) auto-update is disabled; only the
-  install script manages those.
+- **Auto-update assumes a writable home.** v1 installs are user-local, so
+  this holds. If a user relocates via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` to a
+  non-writable location, auto-update detects it and no-ops.
 - **Offline behavior:** auto-update must always no-op gracefully and never
   block or slow a command.
 - **`fastmcp` weight:** bundled for correctness; size revisited only if
   measured and if the MCP backend can stay functional.
 
 ## Left to the builder
 
 - Exact PyInstaller spec / hidden-import hooks and exclusion list.
 - Exact `platformdirs` vs hand-rolled XDG resolution.
 - Exact lockfile mechanism (file lock vs atomic O_EXCL).
 - Windows deferred-swap implementation details.
 - release-please configuration specifics.
 
+## Builder calls made during design review
+
+- **Size threshold:** ~80 MB compressed triggers consideration of lazy
+  `fastmcp`, conditional on the MCP backend surviving in the frozen binary.
+- **First version:** `0.1.0`, pinned explicitly in release-please config.
+- **Installer privilege:** user-local only in v1; no sudo/system-wide path.
+- **Windows updater fallback:** deferred swap, else check-only + explicit
+  `odi update`.
+
 ## Assumptions confirmed by the human partner
 
 1. Keep `agentic-odi` as an alias alongside `odi` / `odipm` / `odi-cli`.
 2. Release assets live on GitHub Releases (`alehar9320/agentic-odi`) for now.
 3. release-please with a single root component (one product version).

import json
import re

import pytest
from fastmcp import Client

from mcp_server import jobs_db, mcp


def extract_id(result_str):
    match = re.search(r'"id"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', result_str)
    return match.group(1) if match else None


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_odi_workflow():
    """Test the full ODI workflow (Add Job -> Add Steps -> Add Outcome -> Get Data)."""
    # Use in-memory testing by passing the server instance directly to the client
    async with Client(mcp) as client:
        # 1. Add a Job
        job_result = await client.call_tool(
            "add_job", {"name": "Listen to music", "description": "Listen to music on the go"}
        )
        job_text = job_result.content[0].text
        assert "Job created successfully" in job_text

        job_id = extract_id(job_text)
        assert job_id in jobs_db

        # 2. Add Steps to the Job Map
        step1_res = await client.call_tool(
            "add_step", {"job_id": job_id, "name": "Select music", "order": 1}
        )
        step2_res = await client.call_tool(
            "add_step", {"job_id": job_id, "name": "Play music", "order": 2}
        )

        step1_text = step1_res.content[0].text
        assert "Step created successfully" in step1_text
        assert "Step created successfully" in step2_res.content[0].text

        step1_id = extract_id(step1_text)

        # 3. Add an Outcome
        outcome_res = await client.call_tool(
            "add_outcome",
            {
                "job_id": job_id,
                "statement": "Minimize the time it takes to find a specific song",
                "importance": 8.5,
                "satisfaction": 4.0,
                "step_id": step1_id,
            },
        )
        outcome_text = outcome_res.content[0].text
        assert "Outcome created successfully" in outcome_text

        outcome_match = re.search(r"({.*})", outcome_text, re.DOTALL)
        outcome_data = json.loads(outcome_match.group(1)) if outcome_match else {}

        # Check that opportunity score was calculated correctly: 8.5 + max(8.5 - 4.0, 0) = 8.5 + 4.5 = 13.0
        assert outcome_data.get("opportunity_score") == 13.0

        # 4. Retrieve Data
        job_map_res = await client.call_tool("get_job_map", {"job_id": job_id})
        job_map_text = job_map_res.content[0].text
        job_map_match = re.search(r"(\[.*\])", job_map_text, re.DOTALL)
        job_map_data = json.loads(job_map_match.group(1)) if job_map_match else []

        assert len(job_map_data) == 2
        assert job_map_data[0]["name"] == "Select music"
        assert job_map_data[1]["name"] == "Play music"

        outcomes_res = await client.call_tool("get_outcomes", {"job_id": job_id})
        outcomes_text = outcomes_res.content[0].text
        outcomes_match = re.search(r"(\[.*\])", outcomes_text, re.DOTALL)
        outcomes_data = json.loads(outcomes_match.group(1)) if outcomes_match else []
        assert len(outcomes_data) == 1
        assert outcomes_data[0]["statement"] == "Minimize the time it takes to find a specific song"


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_get_capabilities():
    """Test that the get_capabilities tool returns the expected human-readable markdown string."""
    async with Client(mcp) as client:
        result = await client.call_tool("get_capabilities", {})
        result_text = result.content[0].text if hasattr(result, "content") else str(result)

        # Check that it returns a string with the expected categories
        assert "Here is what I can help you with" in result_text
        assert "Manage Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)" in result_text
        assert "Build Job Maps" in result_text
        assert "Track Desired Outcomes" in result_text
